title: The house-builder
hook: craving named and seen; the rafters broken, the ridgepole shattered (Dhammapada 153–154)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha: the one who woke up, at dawn, as the morning star rose. Awake.

The same argument, for the tenth time. The same late-night snack. The same reason for not calling someone back. Then one day, instead of just doing it again, you catch it in the act. Oh. There it is. That's the thing that keeps building this. Tradition says that when the Buddha woke, the first words he spoke were a short poem. Not a sermon. Not a rule. A poem to someone he'd been looking for, for a very long time, and finally, he'd found him.
screen: `CATCHING YOURSELF IN A PATTERN.` → `OH. THERE IT IS.` → `A POEM TO SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: The poem is in the Dhammapada, verses one fifty-three and one fifty-four, and it pictures life after life as a house built again and again. Through many births, the Buddha says, he ran on, looking for the builder of this house, and birth again and again was painful. Then, in Max Müller's translation from 1881, he speaks directly to the builder: "maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." Tabernacle is Müller's old word for the house: a dwelling, a tent. And then: "All thy rafters are broken, thy ridge-pole is sundered." So who is the house-builder? The Buddhist commentaries answer: craving. Tanha, the thirst from day nine, the wanting that keeps building a self and a life around it, over and over. The rafters, they say, are the other stains of the mind. The ridgepole, the beam at the very top that holds up the whole roof, is ignorance. And look at the first verb. Before anything is broken, the builder is seen; the rafters fall after. That's this whole week in one poem: a seat of grass, a vow to stay, Mara's army, the earth as witness, three watches, and dawn. And at the end, one quiet sentence to the one who'd been building the whole time. House-builder, you are seen.
screen: `A HOUSE BUILT AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THOU HAST BEEN SEEN.` · `THE BUILDER IS CRAVING.` · `SEEN FIRST, THEN BROKEN.` · then, large: `HOUSE-BUILDER, YOU ARE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Think of one habit you've already started to see through, something you used to do without noticing: hitting snooze, interrupting, checking the fridge when bored. Picture it as a small builder busy with hammer and nails, and silently speak to it the way the poem does, not angrily, just clearly: I see you. Notice whether seeing it changes anything, then rest with the breath.
The house-builder. Craving, which builds life after life, seen at last by the Buddha: its rafters broken, its ridgepole shattered.
Your line: house-builder, you are seen. Day fifty-six closes the night under the tree.

howItsDone: Dhammapada 153–154 are memorized and chanted in Theravada communities, whose tradition holds they were the Buddha's first words after awakening, and teachers use the house-builder to explain craving as the source of rebirth.

original.note: Pali: house-builder (gaha, house + kāraka, maker), the name for craving in Dhammapada 153–154.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem about a broken house.
what it means: the Buddha speaks to craving, the builder of life after life, and says: I see you. you won't build again.
what a scholar hears: gahakāraka in Dhammapada 153–154; the commentary glosses the rafters (phasuka) as defilements and the ridgepole (gahakūṭa) as ignorance.

notes: Two quotations from Max Müller's Dhammapada (SBE X, 1881), verse 154. Check against the 1881 text word for word, including 'ridge-pole' hyphenation and punctuation.
Verse 153 is paraphrased ('looking for the builder... birth after birth was painful').
First words after awakening: the Dhammapada commentary and Theravada tradition; the Vinaya gives the Udana verses instead. The script says 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Commentarial glosses (rafters = defilements, ridgepole = ignorance): confirm.
